Pleasurable sensation associated with the six consciousnesses is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Painful sensation associated with the five [sensory] consciousnesses is called the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
Pleasurable sensation associated with the mental consciousness is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Pain associated with the mental consciousness is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Pain that is neither painful nor pleasant and associated with the six consciousnesses is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Faith in all wholesome phenomena is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Thus, the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
the nine untainted faculties comprised within the path of firm conviction and firm Dharma—these are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
The nine untainted faculties comprised within the paths of faith-liberation and vision-attainment—these are the faculty of "one who has known."
The nine untainted faculties subsumed within the path of no-more-learning constitute the faculty of great knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
What is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)?
To possess power and efficacy is what is called a faculty.
The six faculties, the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life faculty—these nine faculties possess both power and benefit within the world.
The five faculties of sensation (vedanā) possess both power and benefit in the arising of afflictions.
The five faculties, such as faith and the rest, possess both power and benefit within wholesome dharmas.
The three untainted faculties possess both power and benefit within the Path, because they bring about the attainment of the Path.
Each of these faculties possesses its own respective power and benefit.

Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Four faculties are bound to the desire realm:
the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of suffering.
The five faculties bound to the desire and form realms are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties;
the outflow-tainted faculties of joy and pleasure are bound to the desire and form realms.

The faculties of restraint with outflows (*sāsrava*), the mental faculty (*manas*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are all bound to the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) mental faculty, the faculty of restraint, the faculties of joy and pleasure, and the five faculties beginning with faith are not bound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
These nine faculties are subsumed within these three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*):
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
The five faculties beginning with pleasure (*sukha*), the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and all untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties are non-appropriated (*anupātta*);
the remaining faculties are either appropriated or non-appropriated.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Eight faculties are wholesome:
the five beginning with faith and the three untainted faculties. Eight faculties are indeterminate:
the five beginning with the eye faculty, the male faculty, the female faculty, and the life faculty. Six of these require further analysis.

The mind faculty (*manendriya*) and the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), such as pleasure (*sukha*), are either wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The five faculties beginning with faith, as well as pleasure, joy, equanimity, and the mental faculty, are either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
the final three faculties are exclusively uncontaminated.
Ten faculties are contaminated:
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, male, female, life, sorrow, and suffering.
Regarding the three modes of birth, at the very beginning one acquires two faculties:
the body faculty and the life faculty.
Regarding those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there are six, seven, or eight [faculties]: for those without form, there are six;
for those with one sex organ, there are seven;
for those with two sex organs, there are eight—namely, the five beginning with the eye, plus the life-faculty, the male faculty, and the female faculty.
The remaining faculties are acquired in succession.
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one initially acquires six faculties:
the five sensory faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
In the formless realm, one initially acquires a single life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
In the desire realm, when dying with an indeterminate mind, four, eight, nine, or ten faculties cease;
if one dies with a wholesome mind, nine, thirteen, fourteen, or fifteen cease.

Of the twenty-two faculties, how many are abandoned by seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
Four faculties are either abandoned by seeing the truths, abandoned by cultivation, or not to be abandoned:
the mental faculty (*manas*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukha*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is either abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi-pañcendriya*) are either abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned at all.
The three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are not abandoned.
The remaining roots are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Chapter Nine: The Essence of the Abhidharma on the Fetters, Meditations, and Knowledges. Chapter Nine: The Essence of the Abhidharma on the Fetters, Meditations, and Knowledges. There are two ways in which the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned:
abandonment through the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*) and abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Twenty-eight are abandoned through the vision of suffering; nineteen are abandoned through the vision of origination; nineteen are abandoned through the vision of cessation; twenty-two are abandoned through the vision of the path; ten are abandoned through cultivation.

In the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya); seven are abandoned through the vision of origination (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya); seven are abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya); eight are abandoned through the vision of the path (mārga-darśana-prahātavya); and [the remaining] eight are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).

Fourth, there are thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm; excluding ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the remaining underlying tendencies in the form and formless realms each sever thirty-one.
Briefly stated, there are actually ten underlying tendencies:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence (*parāmarśa*), adherence to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), craving (*rāga*), ill-will (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
What is the view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
To conceive of a self within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—such a view is called the view of a self in the body.
To hold that the world is finite or infinite—such a view is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
To hold the view that there are no Four Noble Truths, causes and conditions, or karmic retributions is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
To reckon among tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) that something is permanent and supreme is called the view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To seek the path to purity within causes and conditions that are not pure—such a view is called the "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
To have a mind of delusion regarding the unattained path, failing to discern what is right from wrong or what exists from what does not exist, is called the "mind of doubt and delusion."
Attachment and clinging toward all phenomena is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
When one does not desire within a mind of delusion and the mind becomes agitated with anger upon encountering an opposing object, this is called hatred (*dveṣa*).
An arrogant mind that is conceited is called pride (*māna*).
Not knowing the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas) is called ignorance (avidyā). Regarding these latent tendencies (anuśayas):

in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), there are seven under the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) and all [seven] under the truth of origination (samudayasatya); it is the same for the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya); and there are eight under the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
All wrong views and doubts are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
Four [factors] of the desire realm are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Six [factors] of the form and formless realms are abandoned through cultivation.
Greed, hatred, pride, ignorance, and the five [types of] conduct are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Doubt, wrong view, and the adherence to views are abandoned through the four noble truths (*catuḥ-satya*).
The adherence to a self-identity and the adherence to extremes are abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Path.
Six [factors] of the Desire Realm are abandoned through the Truth of Suffering;
five types of wrong views and doubt are abandoned through the Truth of Origination; three [factors] are abandoned through the Truth of Origination.
The two types—wrong view and doubt, along with ignorance—are abandoned through the realization of the Truth of Suffering.
Ignorance may be pervasive or non-pervasive.
In what sense is it pervasive?
The six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with [other defilements] and unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) are called pervasive (*sarvatraga*). What is non-pervasive?
Ignorance associated with the three underlying tendencies is non-pervasive.

Thus, those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) associated with the three [types of] craving, as well as the unshared ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*); the remaining ones are not pervasive.
Among all latent dispositions, excluding attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*), all others are pervasive.
Why is this? Among these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), five conditions are universal (*sarvatraga*).
Within the latent dispositions, the two types of wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them are universal within their own realm, but not in other realms.
The same applies to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
it is all-pervasive throughout the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are all-pervasive within their own realm are also all-pervasive among the remaining [realms].
The universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of one's own realm also take other realms as their objects.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), both when associated with all other latent dispositions and as independent ignorance, is abandoned through the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path across all three realms.
Wrong view, doubt, and ignorance—these eighteen latent tendencies (anuśaya) have the untainted as their object; the remainder have the tainted as their object.

Those latent tendencies that have the tainted as their object, along with the ignorance associated with them, have the tainted as their object; the remaining ignorance has the untainted as its object.
All fetters and proclivities within the three realms are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Among the various proclivities in the Brahma and Ābhāsvara heavens, they are associated with the faculty of equanimity as well as the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*).
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
The [latent dispositions] bound to the desire realm—namely, wrongness (*mithyātva*), wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)—are associated with three faculties:
the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Doubt is associated with two faculties:
the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of equanimity.
Ill-will is associated with three faculties:
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

As for the remaining [defilements] of the desire realm abandoned by seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), they are associated with two faculties: the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those [defilements] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are associated with the six consciousnesses, with the exception of pride (*māna*), which is associated only with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
All those abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) are associated with the mental consciousness.
The ten minor afflictions are said to be the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*):

first, anger; second, fear of one's own transgressions; third, drowsiness; fourth, sleep; fifth, restlessness; sixth, frivolity; seventh, avarice; eighth, envy; ninth, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); and tenth, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
What is hatred? It is the mind’s movement toward malice and sharpness.
What is fear of one's own faults?
Fearing that others might see or hear [of one's state]. What is sleep?
It is the sinking of the mind, the heaviness of the mind, and the heaviness of the body, associated with all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana*).
What is torpor (*styāna*)?
It is a state of mental lethargy arising from lying down, characterized by a lack of self-mastery, associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
What is agitation (*auddhatya*)?
The unwholesome mind is not autonomous; it is associated with all fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*).
What is frivolity (*auddhatya*)?
It is the regretting of having performed wholesome or unwholesome deeds, and it is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
What is stinginess?
It is a mind that cherishes and begrudges. What is envy?
To feel no joy when seeing others obtain good things, and to wish for them to suffer—
these two fetters (saṃyojana) are bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
What is lack of shame (āhrīkya)?
To commit evil oneself and feel no shame—
how is this not a lack of moral dread? To commit evil and feel no shame before others is what is meant by a lack of moral dread.
These two are associated with all unwholesome dharmas.
The three fetters—
craving, aversion, and ignorance— are associated with the six consciousnesses.
The two types of craving and ignorance pertaining to the form realm are associated with four consciousnesses;
the remaining fetters and proclivities are associated with the mental consciousness, and they are all severed simultaneously by the path of non-obstruction.
Regarding the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), at the time of realization, one realizes them repeatedly.
By severing the fetters of the desire realm, one attains three knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
Those [fetters] of the desire realm to be abandoned through the truth of suffering and the truth of origination constitute one knowledge of abandonment.
The exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by the truth of suffering consists of two knowledges of abandonment.
The exhaustion of those abandoned by the truth of the path consists of three knowledges of abandonment.
The exhaustion of the fetters abandoned by the four truths of the form and formless realms consists of three knowledges of abandonment.
When the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāḥ*) within the desire realm are exhausted, there are seven knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
When those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm are exhausted, there are eight knowledges of abandonment.
When all fetters and afflictions (*sarvasaṃyojanakleśa*) are exhausted, there are nine knowledges of abandonment.
The complete extinction of the fetters without remainder is called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).

It is not the case that there are such fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) that are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*); rather, all of them are associated with the mind.
Why is this? Because the arising of fetters and afflictions destroys wholesome dharmas.
When one observes that wholesome dharmas arise at the time of these fetters, one thereby knows that all fetters are associated with the mind.
All these fetters and latent tendencies are abandoned through two things:
the mind associated with dhyāna and wisdom.
What is abandonment through dhyāna?
First is the pliant mind.
What is wisdom? It is the discernment of all phenomena.
Entering meditative concentration with a single-minded focus to contemplate and reflect upon the impermanence and other characteristics of all phenomena is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
When meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and wisdom proceed together in joint reflection, one attains liberation.
There are three periods:
When practicing virtuous diligence and guarding the mind with one-pointed concentration during seated meditation:
if the mind is pliant, at that time one should contemplate diligence;
if the mind is disciplined, at that time one should contemplate the good with one-pointed mind.
If both of these matters are neither supple nor well-tamed, at that time one should relax the mind and let it go.
It is like a goldsmith who places gold in the fire, sometimes blowing on it with a bellows, sometimes pouring water over it, and sometimes setting it aside to rest.

Why is this? If one blows on gold constantly, it will burn and melt; if one constantly pours water over it, it will remain cold and not heat up; if one leaves it unattended constantly, it will not be refined.

Sitting in meditation is also like this: blowing with a bellows is like diligence (*vīrya*); pouring water is like meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and letting go is like protective restraint (*rakṣā*).

Why is this? Because the mind is constantly disciplined through diligent effort, constantly concentrated through one-pointedness, and constantly guarded so as not to receive [unwholesome] states of mind.
Therefore, by being diligent at times, concentrated at times, and guarding the mind at times, the mind becomes thus harmonized and attains liberation from all fetters and afflictions.

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment and the Immaculate Persons. *Abhidharma-amṛta-rasa*. Chapter Ten: The Method of Seated Meditation. First, bind the mind to a single point—whether at the crown of the head, the center of the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, or the heart—and cause the mind to abide in that one place.
If the mind wanders in thought, one should restrain it and bring it back to settle in each respective object.
This mind is like a monkey; if its neck were tied to a pillar, it would run around the pillar but could not escape, and upon becoming exhausted, it would come to rest.

The wandering of the mind is also like this: when the mind is bound to and attached to the Dharma, it does not depart; once it has reached its limit, it abides. One gradually contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas.

This is entering into the application of mindfulness to dharmas (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), where, through purity and one-pointedness of mind, one attains true wisdom. One contemplates the true mark of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*): they are impermanent because they arise and cease without staying; they are suffering because they accumulate calamities and afflictions; they are empty because there is no person within; and they are non-self because they lack autonomy. From this, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) arises within the mind.
Just as fire is produced from wood when drilled, so too are the pure roots of goodness of faith produced within the Buddha-dharma.
One contemplates the sixteen aspects through four conditions.
Four aspects contemplate the truth of suffering:

Because it arises from causes and conditions and does not abide, it is impermanent; because it is destroyed by the power of impermanence, it is suffering; because it is devoid of a person, it is empty; and because it lacks self-mastery, it is non-self.

One contemplates the Truth of Origination through four aspects: it is the cause of origination because it produces similar effects; it is origination because birth and death continue without interruption; it is existence because it cannot be exhausted; and it is conditionality because there is a dissimilar continuity.
The fourfold contemplation of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*):

it is "cessation" because all suffering and affliction are closed off; it is "stopping" because the fires of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are removed; it is "sublime" because it excels all phenomena; and it is "transcendence" because it goes beyond the three realms.
The fourfold contemplation of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*):

it is the "Path" because it leads to *nirvāṇa*; it is the "Right" because it is not inverted; it is the "Abiding" because it is practiced by the Noble Ones (*ārya*); and it is the "Departure" because it enables one to leave behind worldly afflictions.
To constantly and diligently apply oneself to the sixteen aspects of the wholesome dharmas through contemplation is called the "Heat" stage (*uṣmagata*).

From this, when the wholesome root of Heat increases, becomes superior, and grows, it is called the "Summit" wholesome root (*mūrdhan*); it consists of faith in the Three Jewels, or faith that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Thus, because the supreme *uṣmagata* (heat) dharma takes the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths as its object, it is said that the *mūrdhan* (summit) has increased further.
Following the truths of the *mūrdhan*, there is what is called the *kṣānti* (patience) wholesome root.
This has three types:
Superior, middling, and inferior.
Contemplating the sixteen aspects by means of the four noble truths, these superior roots of goodness that accord with the truths are called the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The mind and its mental concomitants at the moment of "one-pointedness of mind" (ekāgratā) are called the supreme mundane wholesome root (*laukikāgradharma*).

Some say that the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are the supreme mundane dharmas; however, according to the true meaning, it is the mind and its mental concomitants at the moment of one-pointedness of mind that constitute the supreme mundane wholesome root. This is able to open the gate to Nirvāṇa and is the foremost among the dharmas of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). It takes one Truth as its object through four modes of contemplation:
impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
Why is this? Because the first untainted mind takes the Truth of Suffering as its object, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma is likewise.
This pertains to the six stages of dhyāna:

The preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas—these are the roots of goodness of patience (*kṣānti*), the summit (*mūrdhan*), and warmth (*uṣmagata*). Within these six stages, there is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
For one who arises sequentially in the state of the untainted (anāsrava), this is called the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).
Because it is the first time seeing [the truth] and being able to endure it, patience is said to be the beginning.

Following the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) of patience, the "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arises in succession, whereby the characteristics of suffering are known as they truly are.
The path of liberation of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-vimukti-mārga) is of these two [types].

When the mind takes the suffering bound to the desire realm as its object, the path of non-obstruction of subsequent patience (anvaya-kṣānti) and the path of liberation of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) take the suffering bound to the form and formless realms as their objects.
The same applies to the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

These are the sixteen moments of pure mind that constitute the correct contemplation of all phenomena. Among these fifteen moments of mind, those with sharp faculties are said to be "followers by Dharma" (dharmānusārin), while those with dull faculties are said to be "followers by faith" (śraddhānusārin).

These two persons have not yet abandoned the fetters of the desire realm while heading toward the first fruit; they are heading toward the second fruit by abandoning six types of fetters and proclivities of the desire realm, and they are heading toward the third fruit once nine types of fetters are exhausted.

The practitioner who is heading toward the first fruit within the fifteen moments of mind, as well as the practitioner who is progressing through the intermediate fruits—these two, being practitioners by Dharma-following (dharmānusārin) or faith-following (śraddhānusārin), attain and abide in the fruit upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind.
If these two individuals have not previously severed the fetters, they both become Srotāpannas upon completing the sixteen moments of mind.
If they have severed six types of fetters, they both become Sakṛdāgāmins upon completing the sixteen moments of mind.
If one severs nine kinds of fetters and, upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, becomes an Anāgāmin, they attain the third fruit.
When the eighty-eight fetters are exhausted, this person achieves the root of goodness of untainted precepts; therefore, they are called a Srotāpanna.

Those of sharp faculties who attain the fruit are called "those who have seen" (dṛṣṭiprāpta); those of dull faculties who attain the fruit are called "those liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
If these two persons have not yet exhausted the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) bound to the desire realm, they will undergo seven deaths and seven births.
If one has first exhausted three grades [of defilements], this is called a *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family), undergoing three deaths and three births.
The flow of the water of the Eightfold Noble Path leads to *nirvāṇa*; such a person is a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) in progress.
The exhaustion of the six kinds of fetters is called *sakṛdāgāmin*.

The exhaustion of the eight kinds of fetters is called *ekavīcika*; being born among the gods of the desire realm and then returning to be born among humans before attaining parinirvāṇa—this is termed both *ekavīcika* and *sakṛdāgāmin*.
There are five types of Anāgāmins:

those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin), those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin), and those who ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven as an Anāgāmin (ūrdhvasrotas-akaniṣṭhaga).

Furthermore, there are those who attain birth in the formless realm as non-returners (anāgāmin); having exhausted the suffering of the form and formless realms, they attain parinirvāṇa without being reborn in the lower realms—these are called non-returners.
There are nine kinds of fetters and proclivities in the desire realm; it is the same for the form and formless realms. These various fetters and proclivities are abandoned by two paths:
the path of non-obstruction and the path of liberation.
First, one achieves the path of liberation through unimpeded abandonment; this is like catching a venomous snake and placing it in a jar with its mouth covered.

Whether by the mundane path, the supramundane path that transcends the world, or the path of the realms, one abandons the fetters and latent tendencies bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; the mundane path is likewise able to sever the bonds of the higher worlds.
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) while free from desire in the eighth stage is called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) Anāgāmin.
As for an Arhat who is liberated through both parts (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta), the dharma resembling nirvāṇa is manifested within their body.
The exhaustion of the five lower fetters results in the attainment of the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin); the exhaustion of the five higher fetters results in the attainment of Arhatship.
The remaining fetters, proclivities, and entanglements within the realms of form and formlessness—this is called the taming of the mind.

When knowledge of cessation arises in succession to the vajra-like samādhi, at that moment one attains the fruit of arhatship; this is the supreme path of non-obstruction for the abandonment of desire, and it is also the final mind of a trainee (śaikṣa).
This is the sequence of the vajra-samādhi: first, the knowledge of extinction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arises:
"All my births are exhausted and extinguished; I have attained arhatship.
With all fetters (*saṃyojana*) exhausted and all major and minor afflictions (*kleśa*) severed and extinguished, this is called an arhat.
One who is worthy of receiving offerings from all humans and devas is called an Arhat.
There are nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):
first, the one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
2. The one of non-retrogression;
3. The one who contemplates the Dharma;
4. The one who guards the Dharma;
5. The dharma of abiding;
6. The dharma of progress;
7. The dharma of immovability;
8. Liberation through wisdom;
9. dual liberation. What is the "one liable to regression"?
Those with dull wisdom and weak diligence who practice within the five conditions for decline and fall away from the fruits of the path are said to be of the "dharma of decline.
What is the dharma of non-decline?
Those with sharp wisdom and diligent diligence who do not practice within the five conditions for decline and do not fall away from the fruits of the path are said to be of the dharma of non-decline.
What is the contemplation of dharmas?
One of dull wisdom and dull diligence who diligently contemplates the impurity and loathsomeness of the body, reflecting on the extinction of the self-body—this is the contemplation of dharmas.
What is the guarding of the Dharma?
Having gentle wisdom and diligent application of effort, one guards oneself; this is the guarding of the Dharma.
What is the abiding in the Dharma?
Moderate wisdom, moderate diligence, and practicing the Middle Way without increase or decrease—this is the dharma of abiding.
What is the dharma of advancing? Having limited wisdom but diligent diligence, being able to attain immovable goodness—this is the dharma of advancing.
What is the one of immovable dharma?
One who possesses sharp faculties and great diligent effort, having previously attained the immovable wholesome state, is one of immovable dharma.
What is liberation through wisdom?
One who cannot attain the attainment of cessation is one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).
What is one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*)?
One who is able to attain the attainment of cessation is one liberated both ways.
The five types of Arhats who follow by faith are called those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*).
These Arhats possess two knowledges: the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
The one type of arhat who follows the Dharma (dharmanusārin) and possesses sharp faculties is called "one liberated at any time" (asamayavimukta).
This arhat possesses three knowledges:
the knowledge of cessation (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).

The eight types of Arhats—those liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and those who have attained the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*), as well as those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*)—possess nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*); these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
When one attains the fruit through the sixteenth moment of mind, these nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*).
When these same nine faculties are associated with the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are called the faculty of "great knowing" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
When the fruit is attained, the path leading toward it is relinquished; while on the path, the fetters are severed and exhausted, resulting in two kinds of accomplishment:
the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
When the great fruit is attained, all of the original two kinds are relinquished, and one kind of accomplishment is attained.

Regarding the nine types of abandonment of the fetters (saṃyojana) and the non-obscured phenomena (anivṛta-dharma), all are abandoned at the ninth moment of mind. One who is capable of progress (pratipannaka-dharma) attains the immovable wholesome state (akopya-kuśala) as an Arhat, and none other. A learner (śaikṣa) liberated by faith (śraddhādhimukta) who attains sharp faculties is called one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and none other.

Within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are each distinct, and the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*) are each distinct. For this reason, one sees the truths gradually; they are not seen all at once. One attains the fruit through the power of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*). For this reason, there are two kinds of fruits:
conditioned fruits (*saṃskṛtaphala*) and unconditioned fruits (*asaṃskṛtaphala*).

Chapter Eleven, The Chapter on Knowledge (Jñāna-varga). The Ten Knowledges (*daśa-jñānāni*):

knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), knowledge of extinction (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?

It is the untainted knowledge regarding the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the origin of all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm; and, because one abandons the path leading to the cessation of all conditioned phenomena bound to the desire realm, the untainted knowledge regarding that path and the untainted knowledge within the stage of the knowledge of phenomena—this is called the knowledge of phenomena.

What is the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*)? It is the untainted knowledge regarding the suffering of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness; the untainted knowledge regarding the origin of all conditioned phenomena bound to the realms of form and formlessness; the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of all conditioned phenomena bound to the realms of form and formlessness; the untainted knowledge regarding the path that abandons all conditioned phenomena bound to the realms of form and formlessness; the untainted knowledge within the path; and the untainted knowledge within the stage of the knowledge of the unknown—this is called the knowledge of the unknown.
What is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
All contaminated wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*), whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, is called conventional knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?

Through the power of contemplation within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one attains knowledge of the minds and mental factors of others within the desire realm; this is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
It is the untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom that contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*)?

It is the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that contemplates the origination, cause, existence, and conditions of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*); this is called the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of cessation (*kṣaya-jñāna*)?
The untainted wisdom that contemplates exhaustion, cessation, the sublime, and transcendence is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
Abiding in the Eightfold Noble Path and observing with outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) for the sake of transcendence—this is called the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)?
Seeing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing its cessation, and contemplating the path—observing these four dharmas with outflow-free wisdom—this is called the knowledge of cessation.

What is the knowledge of non-arising? It is the untainted wisdom that contemplates these four dharmas: "I have already seen suffering and shall not see it again; I have already abandoned its origin and shall not abandon it again; I have already realized its cessation and shall not realize it again; I have already cultivated the path and shall not cultivate it again. This is called the knowledge of non-arising.
Among these ten knowledges, two knowledges possess sixteen aspects:
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Within the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) possesses sixteen aspects; within the Worldly Supreme Dharma, it possesses four aspects; the remaining [knowledges] possess no aspects.
The untainted knowledge of others' minds has four aspects, as does the knowledge of the path; the tainted knowledge of others' minds has no aspects.

The knowledge of suffering has four aspects, the knowledge of origin has four aspects, the knowledge of cessation has four aspects, and the knowledge of the path has four aspects. The knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of non-arising each have fourteen aspects, excluding the aspects of emptiness and non-self.

In the stages of the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), there are nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds. In the remaining four dhyānas, there are ten knowledges.
In the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there are eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The first untainted mind accomplishes one knowledge:
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). The second untainted mind accomplishes three knowledges:
The knowledge of equality, the knowledge of phenomena, and the knowledge of suffering;
the third untainted mind passes beyond;
the fourth untainted mind accomplishes four knowledges:
The conventional knowledge, the dharma-knowledge, the knowledge of suffering, and the subsequent knowledge;
this is the fifth supramundane mind.
Upon the sixth supramundane mind, one accomplishes five knowledges:
The knowledge of equality, the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of what is yet to be known, and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the origin [of suffering];
the seventh untainted mind has passed;
the eighth untainted mind has also passed.
The ninth untainted mind accomplishes six knowledges:
conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, knowledge of suffering, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of origin, and knowledge of cessation;
the tenth and eleventh untainted minds transcend these.
The twelve types of untainted consciousness accomplish seven knowledges:
conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, knowledge of suffering, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path.
If one has already become free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds increases.
There are two ways of cultivating knowledge: cultivation through acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and cultivation through practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).

That which was not previously attained and is now attained is called cultivation through acquisition; that which was previously attained and now manifests before one is called cultivation through practice.
That which is cultivated while manifesting within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) is precisely what is to be cultivated in the future;
likewise, the various patiences (kṣānti) cultivated while manifesting are also to be cultivated in the future.

Within the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)—namely, the subsequent knowledge of suffering, the subsequent knowledge of origin, and the subsequent knowledge of cessation—one cultivates conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
Within the path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*), one cultivates either six or seven knowledges:
if one has not yet abandoned desire, one cultivates six knowledges; if one has already abandoned desire, one cultivates seven knowledges.
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) transcends the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).

Within the seventeen moments of mind, seven knowledges are cultivated, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).

When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) attains sharp faculties within these seventeen moments of mind, six knowledges are cultivated during both the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), excluding the knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of non-arising.

Upon attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*, one cultivates eight knowledges within the path of liberation, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Likewise, when becoming free from desire in the seven stages [of the form realm], one cultivates eight knowledges within the path of liberation, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of non-arising.
This is called cultivating seven knowledges within the path of non-obstruction, excluding the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of non-arising.

When becoming free from desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one cultivates seven knowledges within the eight paths of liberation, excluding conventional knowledge, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of non-arising.

Within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), six knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Within the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*), all wholesome roots (*kuśala-mūla*), both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), are cultivated; this first mind of one beyond training is associated with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-jñāna*).
Some say it is associated with the knowledge of the unknown (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Why? Because it is associated with the conditions for rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

The initial mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*)—the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) during the vision of the truths—is called "vision" (*darśana*) and not "knowledge" (*jñāna*), because it is characterized by seeking and investigation. The knowledge of cessation (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are "knowledge" and not "vision.

All remaining untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is both "wisdom" (*prajñā*), "vision," and "knowledge," with the exception of wholesome tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-kuśala-prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-samprayukta*) and the five false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The remaining contaminated wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) is both knowledge (*jñāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), but it is not vision (*dṛṣṭi*).

The dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) has nine knowledges as its objects, excluding the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). The subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) has nine knowledges as its objects, excluding the dharma-knowledge.
The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) has nine knowledges as its objects, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudayajñāna*) have all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as their objects; the remaining knowledges have all ten knowledges as their objects.

Conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have two knowledges as their objects:

Exhaustion-knowledge (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*). Path-dharma-knowledge (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) can extinguish the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms; it constitutes six of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), namely four of them.

Equality-knowledge (*sāmānya-jñāna*) consists of the superknowledge of the body (*kāya-abhijñā*), the superknowledge of the ear (*śrotra-abhijñā*), the superknowledge of the eye (*cakṣus-abhijñā*), the superknowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*), and the superknowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-abhijñā*).
The five knowledges are:

knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna). The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-abhijñā) consists of nine uncontaminated knowledges (anāsrava-jñāna), excluding conventional knowledge.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness of the body consists of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of exhaustion.
The foundation of mindfulness of feelings and the foundation of mindfulness of the mind consist of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion.
The application of mindfulness to phenomena consists of ten knowledges.
The four analytical knowledges— analytical knowledge of phenomena, analytical knowledge of expression, and so forth— are conventional knowledge.
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*) each consist of ten knowledges (*jñāna*).

The knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhi-jñāna*) consists of seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Regarding the ten powers (*bala*), the first power is known by all ten knowledges.
The second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth powers consist of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
The seventh power consists of ten knowledges.
The eighth and ninth powers consist of one knowledge, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The ten powers consist of nine knowledges, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The first fearlessness is known by all ten knowledges.
The second fearlessness is known by nine knowledges, excluding conventional knowledge.
The three fearlessnesses are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of the path and the knowledge of exhaustion.
The four fearlessnesses are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin.

Chapter 12: On Meditative Concentration (Dhyāna) The Essence of the Abhidharma: Chapter Twelve on Meditative Concentration One who attains meditative concentration achieves one-pointedness of mind; the mind does not scatter, and wisdom becomes pure. It is like an oil lamp placed where there is no wind, shining with clear purity.
What is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? There are eight types of meditative concentration:
the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
The four dhyānas:
the first dhyāna and the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Among these various meditative concentrations (dhyāna-samādhi), three types of dhyāna are characterized by relish (āsvāda) and purity (śuddha).

That which is associated with outflow-free craving is called "with relish" (*āsvādana*); wholesome, outflow-possessing dhyāna is called "pure" (*śuddha*); that which is free from afflictions is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

Within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are two kinds of meditative absorption: those with relish and those that are pure; there is no outflow-free meditative absorption or wholesome dharma therein.

Sitting in a secluded and quiet place—whether standing, reclining, walking, or pacing—one should enter meditative concentration with a concentrated mind, skillful wisdom, and a heart of gentle faith; in this manner, the mind should enter *dhyāna*.

The desire, diligence, mindfulness, wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind associated with dhyāna—these wholesome factors lead to the first dhyāna concentration. It is the state free from sensual desires and free from evil, unwholesome states; accompanied by directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra); born of seclusion from desire, and characterized by joy and bliss. This is called the first dhyāna.
Attachment to external sense bases is called sensual desire; ill will, sloth, torpor, restlessness, agitation, and doubt—these hindrances are called evil, unwholesome states.
The abandonment of these two types of internal and external unwholesome dharmas is called "separation" (*viveka*).

The turning of the mind toward the object is called "applied thought" (*vitarka*); the mental engagement and reflection upon it is called "sustained thought" (*vicāra*). The attainment of dhyāna through the power of abandoning evil and unwholesome dharmas is called "detachment" (*virāga*). The arising of joy in the mind is called "joy" (*prīti*); the tranquility of body and mind is called "bliss" (*sukha*); and the binding of the mind within the object is called "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*). These are the five factors of the first dhyāna.

Sensual desire is a great suffering and a sinful state that brings no joy; through the power of renunciation, one finds peace and liberation. Contemplating sensual desires and other such things in this way, various wholesome dharmas arise within the mind; this is called attaining the path of the first dhyāna.
These three feeling-faculties (vedanendriya) are associated with the faculties of joy (saumanasya), pleasure (sukha), and equanimity (upekṣā).
The faculty of pleasure is associated with the three groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya).

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); the mental consciousness is associated with it; and the four [other] consciousnesses are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
This first dhyāna possesses both distinct bodies and distinct perceptions, as well as a distinct body and a single perception.
The four minds:

the eye, ear, body, and mind of the first dhyāna—this is called the first dhyāna. When all applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have ceased, there is internal purity and one-pointedness of mind; being free from applied and sustained thought, it is associated with the joy and bliss born of concentration—this is called the second dhyāna.
Vitarka and vicāra are as previously explained.
Their abandonment is called cessation.
The stainless faith in all stages is called internal purity.
The state in which the mental consciousness is bound to its object without distraction is called "one-pointedness of mind.
The factors of joy and bliss are as previously explained.
These two are associated with the two faculties of sensation (*vedanā-indriya*).
The faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). When there is a single perception of the body as distinct [from the mind], it is associated with the faculty of joy.
In the fundamental dhyānas and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), it is associated with the faculty of equanimity.

Eliminating the defilements of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and eliminating the conceptualization of meritorious qualities—this is the path leading to the second dhyāna, because it is free from the defilement of joy (*prīti*).

For one who guards their practice and experiences physical bliss (*kāyika-sukha*) while remaining untainted (*anāsrava*), this is called "blissful guarding of mindfulness" as they enter the third dhyāna through that lower bliss.
Detachment from joy is as previously explained.

Regarding the pleasure of guarding the mind and the pleasure of equanimity (*upekṣā*), these two types of painful and pleasant sensations do not cause affliction. One dwells with mindfulness and clear comprehension within this bodily pleasure; because this pleasure is difficult to know as a true dharma, it is therefore called "pleasure" in the context of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
One also practices the guarding of desire and other wholesome dharmas; this path leads to the third dhyāna.
One contemplates the fault of joy as something not to be delighted in, and delights in contemplating the dhyāna.

Equanimity (upekṣā), happiness (sukha), mindfulness (smṛti), clear comprehension (samprajanya), and one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā)—these are called the five factors, as explained previously.
This is called the third dhyāna.

Having abandoned pleasure and pain and previously extinguished the faculties of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna with equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, along with other wholesome dharmas such as desire for the good.
Furthermore, observing that pleasure and pain are defilements and that there is neither suffering nor pleasure, one skillfully abides; this is the path for entering the fourth dhyāna.
The four factors are:
mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, and one-pointedness of mind; through the power of dhyāna, the breath ceases—this is called the fourth dhyāna.
All dhyāna factors are wholesome.

In the stage of *anāgamya-dhyāna* (the preparatory stage), there is both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is no applied thought but sustained thought remains. These two stages are associated with the guarding of the faculties (*indriya-rakṣa*).
The stage of *anāgamya-dhyāna* is of two kinds:
pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), but not of the nature of relish (*āsvādana*).
Within the four dhyānas there are three types:
the savored (āsvādana), the pure (śuddha), and the untainted (anāsrava).
These are called the dharmas of dhyāna.

Detaching from the recollection of form, one also contemplates immeasurable space; entering the concentration of space, one contemplates the defilements of form and attains skillful stillness in the sphere of space, observing this path as leading to the concentration of space.

Recollecting immeasurable consciousness, one enters the sphere of consciousness; contemplating the defilements of the sphere of space and attaining skillful stillness in the sphere of consciousness, one observes this path as leading to the concentration of consciousness.

The practice of infinite consciousness is suffering; recollecting the sphere of nothingness, one enters the concentration of nothingness. One contemplates the defilements of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the wholesome stillness of the sphere of nothingness; contemplating this path leads to the concentration of nothingness.

There is sickness in the sphere of perception and delusion in the sphere of non-perception; contemplating thus, one enters the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. One contemplates the defilement of the sphere of nothingness and the wholesome stillness of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; contemplating this path as leading to the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this is called the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
There are two paths leading to Nirvana:
first, contemplating the impurity of the body;
second, mindfulness of breathing.

Within the applications of mindfulness of the body, there are the first two liberations; within the four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the impure dharmas are explained in detail; entering meditative concentration through counting the breaths from one and two up to ten recollections; guarding the inhalation and exhalation like a gatekeeper; and contemplating the arising and ceasing of all phenomena—these are the sixfold distinctions of the two characteristics and their specific characteristics.

One contemplates the body as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; contemplating all phenomena in this same way, one fears the world and gradually eliminates defilements, practicing wholesome dharmas until reaching nirvana.
In the stages of the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there are two types:
contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
At the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all contaminated states consist of the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*):
The contemplations on impermanence, suffering, suffering as selfless, the loathsomeness of food, the lack of delight in all worlds, impurity, death, relinquishment, dispassion, and cessation.
To recollect that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent is called the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
To recollect that the world is filled with suffering such as birth and so forth is called the perception of suffering (*dukkhasaññā*).
To recollect that both internally and externally there is impermanence, suffering, lack of self-mastery, and emptiness is called the perception of suffering and non-self (*dukkha-anattasaññā*).
To recollect how food is obtained through much toil and suffering, and how it is impure when being eaten—this is called the perception of the repulsiveness of food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*).

To recollect the fears of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and how various afflictions fill the world—this is called the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in (*sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñā*).
To contemplate the actual reality within oneself is called the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).
To recollect that all who are born must inevitably die is called the perception of death (*maraṇa-saṃjñā*).
To recollect the cessation of all afflictions and their thorough stilling is called the perception of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃjñā*).
To recollect impermanence and detachment from desire is called the perception of non-desire.
To recollect that the five aggregates of clinging will not arise again, and to recollect their exhaustion, cessation, excellence, relinquishment, and nirvana, is called the perception of exhaustion.
By constantly recollecting these ten perceptions, one attains the end of suffering.

Chapter Thirteen: Miscellaneous Concentration (*Saṃkīrṇa-samādhi-varga*). The Flavor of the Ambrosia of Abhidharma. Chapter Thirteen: Miscellaneous Concentration. Samādhis, etc., which pervade all bases, including the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and dhyāna.
The three samādhis:
the emptiness samādhi, the wishlessness samādhi, and the signlessness samādhi.
Because the mind is bound to an object that is untainted (anāsrava), these are called samādhis.
To single-mindedly contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as empty, non-self, and not belonging to a self is called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
To enter this concentration and not wish for lust, anger, or delusion to arise again is called the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
This samādhi takes as its object the departure from the ten perceptions (*saṃjñā*).
What are the ten perceptions?
They are: the five sense objects such as form, male, female, birth, old age, and impermanence.
This is called the samādhi of non-perception.
The samādhi of emptiness has two modes of practice:
the mode of emptiness and the mode of non-self.
The wishless samādhi has ten modes of practice: the modes of impermanence, suffering, and the path of cultivation.
The signless samādhi has four modes of practice, which exhaust [the outflows].
The four immeasurables:
Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
When one attains happiness oneself, one should contemplate bestowing it upon all sentient beings.
This involves three kinds of mind:
First one contemplates one's own close relatives, next those who are neutral, and finally enemies and thieves.

With single-minded attention, one reflects that the bodies of all sentient beings in the three realms and one's enemies are no different. By eliminating internal anger, one brings forth the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This enables the arising of right speech and right action, as well as other formations not associated [with anger]. This is called "loving-kindness and its associates."

With single-minded reflection, one contemplates the various sufferings of body and mind experienced by sentient beings within the three realms, desiring to deliver and rescue them; such contemplation is able to eliminate external afflictions. This compassion and its associated aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness can give rise to right speech and right action, as well as other non-associated formations; this is what is meant by "compassion and its associates."

With single-minded contemplation, one reflects on how the sentient beings of the three realms joyfully obtain happiness and are able to eliminate sorrow and suffering. The sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with such joy, as well as the ability to give rise to right speech and right action, along with all other formations that are not so associated—these are called "joy and its associates."

With single-minded contemplation, one reflects upon the pleasure and pain of sentient beings within the three realms, rejoicing in their happiness and wishing to protect them so as to eliminate desire and hatred; this includes the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness associated with such protection, as well as the ability to give rise to right speech and right action, along with all other formations not associated with them—this is called "protection and so forth."

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are: the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhividhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), knowledge of the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), and the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
With the exception of the sixth power, the remaining ones may also be attained by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
What is the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna)? It is of three kinds:
first, flying; second, transformation; and third, the supernormal power of the noble ones (ārya-ṛddhi).
There are three kinds of flight:
first, moving by one's own body like a flying bird;
second, suddenly disappearing from this land and arriving in another realm.
Third, mastery over the power of the mind is like bending or extending one's arm;
this is called the supernormal power (abhijñā) of the Buddhas, not that of other paths.
Constantly contemplating the emptiness of the body and training in levitation—this path leads to supernormal powers.

The ability to become large or small, to make much from little and little from much, and to transform into various kinds of objects, is called the supernormal power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-ṛddhi*).
The transformations of ordinary persons last for seven days at most; after seven days, they perish.

The Buddhas and their disciples transform with mastery: when transforming, they may perceive the pure as impure or the impure as pure, provided they maintain mindfulness and mental protection regarding these notions of purity and impurity. This is called the supernormal power of the noble ones (*ārya-ṛddhi*).

These three types of supernormal powers arise from the power of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); through the gradual cultivation of all material objects as conditions, one attains lightness and levity.

The Buddhas attain them instantaneously. Regarding the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): from the side of one’s own eyes, one produces the pure [organ] made of the four great elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and thereby attains the divine eye. One perceives clearly through the earth below, whether near or far, seeing all subtle and minute forms; by recollecting the sun, moon, stars, fire, and bright jewels, one attains the supernormal power of the divine eye through this path.

The supernormal power of the divine ear: from one’s own ear, through the production of a purified form derived from the four great elements of the form realm, one attains the divine ear; one recollects, perceives, and knows the various sounds of devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—this is the path leading to the supernormal power of the divine ear.

The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives consists of remembering former existences and the places from which one has come to be born; this is the path leading to the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives.

The supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others consists of constantly reflecting upon and fully knowing the defiled minds and pure minds of others, as well as being able to discern and know the arising and ceasing of one's own mind; this is the path leading to the supernormal knowledge of knowing the minds of others.

When all outflows (āsrava) within the three realms have been exhausted by me, and one thus recollects the impermanence and other characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha), this is the path for attaining the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna), the divine eye (divyacakṣus), and the exhaustion of outflows—these are called the "clear knowledges" (vidyā).
Specifically, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives that knows the sequence of causes and conditions across successive lifetimes is called a clear knowledge.
The supernormal power of the divine eye, which knows the causes and conditions by which one receives retribution according to one's karma, is called clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, wherein one thinks, "In the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, my outflows are exhausted; I have exhausted all outflows," is called clear knowledge.
The ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*): recollecting all earth and not recollecting anything else is called the totality of earth;
this applies likewise up to the totality of consciousness.

The eight liberations are: possessing the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; not possessing the perception of internal forms while perceiving external forms; the liberation of the beautiful, which is realized; the four formless attainments; and the attainment of cessation. These are called the eight liberations.
Liberation of the mind through the turning of contemplative observation is called liberation.
Contemplating the impurity of internal form and contemplating external form is called the first liberation.
Not contemplating internal form while contemplating the impurity of external form is the second liberation.
Discerning all pure forms internally and externally is the third liberation.
The four formless attainments are the [next] four liberations.
The liberation of cessation.
Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few, whether beautiful or ugly; this is the first liberation based on superior knowledge and vision.
Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly; this is the second liberation based on superior knowledge and vision.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited, whether beautiful or ugly; this, through superior knowledge and vision, is the third sphere of liberation (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly; this, through superior knowledge and vision, is the fourth sphere of liberation.
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as blue; this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), characterized by superior knowledge and vision.
The same applies to yellow, red, and white.
Without removing the perception of internal forms, one contemplates a small amount of pure external form; this is the first immeasurable object (*apramāṇālambana*).
Second, having internally removed the perception of form, one contemplates externally the purification of limited forms; third, the immeasurable objects of focus;
fourth, the recollection of other colors such as blue, yellow, red, and white.
Because these four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) possess superior purity as their object of focus, they are called "bases of mastery."
Having a beautiful form and upright appearance, one is liberated through the removal of defilements; this is called the *vibhūta-āyatana* (sphere of mastery).
These are distinct in name.
The three liberations (*vimokṣa*), the four spheres of mastery, and the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are subsumed within the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
The ten knowledges are as previously explained.
The three types of compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā), as well as the five supernormal powers (abhijñā), exist within the fundamental four dhyānas.
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) exists within six stages.

The preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), joy (*prīti*), and so forth, as well as the first and second liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Among these, the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the remaining spheres of mastery within the first and second dhyānas are included.

The pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*) and the eight bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) exist within the fourth dhyāna; the remaining liberations and two bases of totality are subsumed under their own respective names.
The liberation of cessation (*nirodha-vimokṣa*) is subsumed within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

The three samādhis, the seven knowledges, and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows are subsumed within nine stages, excluding the conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Within ten stages, there are the three liberations of the formless realm, which may be either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); the remaining three liberations, the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are with outflows.
In the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), all contaminated states (*sāsrava*) are dull and not swift; therefore, they are contaminated.
In the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is no wisdom; therefore, it is contaminated.

Among the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), there is mostly indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*); since the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) take sentient beings as their object, they are thus with outflows (*sāsrava*).
If desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms are fully present;
if desire for the realm of sensuality is already exhausted, the fetters of the realms of form and formlessness remain fully present.

When craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*) is exhausted, the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are no longer established. When craving for the formless realm is exhausted, the fetters and proclivities of all three realms are no longer established.
When craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is exhausted, the pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna is established.
In all such stages, the noble ones achieve the untainted (*anāsrava*).
When a noble one is born in a higher or lower stage, they achieve the untainted.
Having sought and attained the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the four immeasurables (*brahmavihāra*), the fetters and defilements of the lower stages are no longer achieved.
The mundane path relies on the stage of *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) dhyāna to become detached from the desires of the lower stages;
likewise, all untainted (*anāsrava*) paths rely on the fundamental dhyāna stages to become detached from the desires of their own stage as well as those of the higher stages.

Since this is the case for all stages, ordinary persons cannot become free from desire within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); rather, it is through the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that one becomes free from desire.
A person cultivates impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) at two times:
the present and the future.

Within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), during the moments of the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-ājñendriya*), one cultivates untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) as it manifests in the present.
Regarding the future, there are two kinds:
contaminated and uncontaminated knowledge.
Within the remaining moments of mind that are presently manifest, there is both the present uncontaminated and the future uncontaminated.

If a disciple of the Blessed One, having become detached from sensual desire, brings the stage of access concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) into presence and cultivates the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*), they cultivate both paths with and without outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*) in the future.

In the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates the contaminated path in the present, while in the future one cultivates both the contaminated and uncontaminated first dhyāna, as well as the uncontaminated threshold dhyāna (*anāgamya*).
If one relies on the threshold dhyāna, one cultivates the uncontaminated path in the present, while in the future one cultivates both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths.
In the ninth path of liberation, one manifests and cultivates the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) in the present, while cultivating both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted paths in the future.

If a disciple of the Blessed One, having become detached from the craving for the first dhyāna, relies on the stage of the threshold of the second dhyāna (*anāgamya*), they manifest and cultivate the tainted path in the present, while cultivating both tainted and untainted paths in the future.
In the ninth path of liberation, one practices the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) as it manifests in the present, while practicing the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) in the future.

Regarding the three types of first dhyāna and the cultivation of the pure and uncontaminated second dhyāna: if one is free from craving for the first dhyāna and proceeds to the second dhyāna by means of the uncontaminated path, one cultivates the uncontaminated path of one's own level (*svabhūmi*) and both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths of other levels (*parabhūmi*).
In the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) as it manifests in the present, and cultivates the untainted [path] for the future.

This includes the three types of first dhyāna—pure (*śuddha*), untainted (*anāsrava*), and so forth—as well as the pure and untainted second dhyāna, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The same applies to the detachment from desire.
