When one becomes detached from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one cultivates all untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

Within the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one cultivates the untainted path in the present; in the future, one cultivates the untainted as well as twenty-three kinds of wholesome roots (*kuśala-mūla*) bound to the three realms and their respective concentrations.

There are eight types of pure (śuddha) with outflows (sāsrava), eight types of untainted (anāsrava), and seven types that are entirely untainted. Regarding the untainted factors of the seven stages, they are natural causes (svabhāva-hetu) for the untainted factors of their own stage.
Untainted factors of one's own stage have three kinds of causes:
associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu), co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), and natural cause (svabhāva-hetu).
The first dhyāna with outflow is caused by the first dhyāna with outflow and not by any other cause.
The first pure dhyāna is caused by the first pure dhyāna and not by any other cause.
From the first untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), six kinds of concentrations arise in succession:
the first dhyāna is of two types—pure (*śuddha*) and untainted; likewise for the second and third dhyānas.
The untainted second dhyāna arises in succession from eight stages: two from its own stage, four from the higher stages, and two from the lower stages.

The untainted third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space arise in succession from ten stages: four from the higher stages, four from the lower stages, and two from their own stage.
From the untainted consciousness sphere (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nine states arise in succession: three from the higher stage, four from the lower stages, and two from its own stage.
From the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana* samādhi), seven states arise in succession: one from the higher stage, four from the lower stages, and two from its own stage.
The fourth formless attainment successively gives rise to six: four from the lower stages and two from its own stage.
The pure dhyāna is also like this.
The "savoring" [attainment] successively gives rise to two: the savoring of its own stage and also the pure.

In this way, all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of all stages—whether pure (*śuddha*), untainted (*anāsrava*), having all as their object, or having all phenomena as their object—are associated with attachment to their own stage; yet, when they take their own stage as an object while being associated with attachment, they are likewise pure.
Because they have a taste for existence (*sāsvāda*), they cannot take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;

nor can they take the pure (*śubha*) as their object. Untainted formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) do not take tainted stages as their objects. Formless attainments with a taste for existence take the "taste" of their own stage as their object, as well as the pure, but they cannot take the untainted as their object.
The four immeasurables, the eight bases of mastery, the three liberations, and the eight bases of totality—all these dharmas have the entire desire realm as their object.
The five supernormal powers have both the desire and form realms as their objects.
All dhyānas are perfumed by the outflow-free (anāsrava) dhyāna; the outflow-free dhyāna perfumes the outflow-possessing (sāsrava) dhyānas.
One who attains the four dhyānas first perfumes the fourth dhyāna and subsequently perfumes the three lower dhyānas, thereby obtaining rebirth in the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
The Arhat of Immovable Dharma attains all meditative concentrations; he is able to attain the "summit" concentration, and is able both to prolong his lifespan and to relinquish it.

Through the wisdom of aspiration, which follows whatever is wished for from the mind, he fully knows all phenomena of the past, future, and present, and possesses extensive knowledge of future phenomena.

The four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are: the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
Causing the minds of others not to give rise to anger is called "non-contention" (*araṇā*); it is subsumed within the four dhyānas and also exists in the desire realm.
The knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) is subsumed under the fourth dhyāna, as well as the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmanirukti-pratisaṃvid) and the analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid) are subsumed under the desire realm and among the Brahmās; the remaining two analytical knowledges are subsumed under nine stages (bhūmi).
There are two occasions for the pure dhyānas of the desire realm, the four dhyānas, and the four formless attainments:
the time of attaining detachment from desire and the time of attaining rebirth.
There are two occasions for attaining dhyāna with relish:
There are two kinds of attainment regarding the attainment of the untainted dhyānas:
attainment at the time of falling back and attainment through the separation from desire.
The ninth stage encompasses the uncontaminated [states] capable of severing the fetters and latent tendencies.
There are fourteen minds of transformation:
ten minds of the form realm and four minds of the desire realm.
The first dhyāna has two transformation-minds:
one of the first dhyāna and one of the desire realm.
The second dhyāna has three transformation-minds:
The second dhyāna has one; the first dhyāna has one; and the desire realm has one.
The third dhyāna has four transformation-minds:
one from the third dhyāna, one from the second dhyāna, one from the first dhyāna, and one from the desire realm.
The fourth dhyāna possesses five transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*):
one from the fourth dhyāna, one from the third dhyāna, one from the second dhyāna, one from the first dhyāna, and one from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Whichever dhyāna has been accomplished, its resultant transformation-mind of a lower stage is accomplished while one dwells in the stage of the third dhyāna; when the consciousness of the Brahma-heaven manifests, one is able to see and hear, at which time it is accomplished, and when that [consciousness] ceases, it is no longer accomplished.

14. The Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment: The Ambrosial Essence of Abhidharma, Chapter Fourteen. Mindfulness, Right Effort, the Bases of Psychic Power, the Faculties, the Powers, the Factors of Enlightenment, and the Path—these seven factors lead to Nirvāṇa.
Among these, the seven factors of enlightenment are untainted (*anāsrava*); the six [factors] should be distinguished as being either tainted or untainted. Some say:
"The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path are all untainted; the remainder should be distinguished."
The four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are included within all stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).
Constantly maintaining mindfulness through the four kinds of knowledge is called "mindfulness" (smṛti).
The three kinds of mindfulness involve the exercise of wisdom within the body; this is called "mindfulness of the body" (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
In this way, there are the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, the mind, and phenomena; these are called the four foundations of mindfulness.
For what reason are three foundations of mindfulness or five foundations of mindfulness not taught?
The four foundations of mindfulness are taught for the purpose of destroying the four perversions.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of the body?
It is for the purpose of destroying the perversion of the notion of purity.
One contemplates the true characteristics of the body as the thirty-six impurities—such as the corpse, worms, putrefaction, and remaining bones.
By contemplating the body in this way, the perversion of perceiving it as pure is destroyed.

What is the application of mindfulness to feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*)? One contemplates that all feelings—whether arising, abiding, or ceasing—are suffering. Within pleasant feeling lies the underlying tendency of sensual desire; within painful feeling, the underlying tendency of aversion; and within neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency of ignorance. One contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. This is called the application of mindfulness to feeling.
What is the application of mindfulness to the mind?

It is the contemplation of the defiled mind and the undefiled mind, whether the mind is concentrated or distracted, and the contemplation of suffering, impermanence, and so forth; this is called the application of mindfulness to the mind.

What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)? It is observing internal phenomena, observing external phenomena, and observing both internal and external phenomena; observing past and future phenomena; observing how many of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been abandoned and how many have not been abandoned; and observing suffering and impermanence, observing the causal conditions of origination, and observing cessation and tranquility. This is called the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
What are the four right efforts?
When evil and unwholesome states arise in the mind, one desires to eliminate them, exerting diligence and vigor to restrain the mind and abide in wholesome states;
when evil and unwholesome states have not yet arisen, one strives with diligence and vigor so that they do not arise, restraining the mind to abide in wholesome states.
Desiring that unarisen wholesome dharmas arise, one dwells with diligence and vigor;
desiring that arisen wholesome dharmas not be lost but rather increase and expand, one dwells with diligence and vigor—these are called the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*).
What are the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

They are the concentration of desire, the concentration of vigor, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation. From these, one attains all meritorious qualities; these are called the four bases of spiritual power.
Desiring to definitively sever all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and achieve the foremost supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*):
this "desire" refers to aspiration; this "concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the non-diffusion of the mind.

Desire, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, joy, and tranquility—these are called the conditioned formations conjoined with desire and concentration. Thus, because one applies vigor, mind, and wisdom through desire and great desire in order to attain concentration, it is called "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*).
Such diligence, mind, and wisdom are called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Within the four unshakable faiths, there is faith; this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The four kinds of mental diligence are called the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*).
Maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness within the four foundations of mindfulness is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
One-pointedness of mind within the four dhyānas is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
The wisdom within the Four Noble Truths is called the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
Being fundamental, sharp, swift, and supreme—this is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
The five powers, such as faith and the rest, which cannot be destroyed by evil or unwholesome states, are called "powers" (*bala*).
The small is the faculty (*indriya*); the great is the power (*bala*).
Mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—these are called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
What is mindfulness?
To be mindful of the various faults of conditioned phenomena arising and ceasing, and of Nirvana as supremely wondrous—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.
To analytically contemplate therein—this is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena.
Among these, the diligent application of effort through contemplation is called the awakening factor of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Among these, the joy and rapture derived from attaining the flavor of wholesome dharmas is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Among these, the contemplation wherein body and mind become light, supple, and tranquil, following meditative concentration, is called the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Among these, the concentration of the mind through causes and conditions so that it remains undisturbed is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Among these, the relaxation of the mind, its cessation, non-attention, and lack of desire is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Attaining the power of meditative concentration through various forms of wisdom and thereby eliminating all afflictions—this is called the fruit of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
The severing of all afflictions through the seven factors, such as mindfulness and the rest, is termed "enlightenment" (*bodhi*).
Right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right effort, and right concentration—these are called the Eightfold Noble Path.
True wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths is called right view.
Within this, the three types of mental application—wholesomeness, non-anger, and non-harming—are called right intention.
The abandonment of the four kinds of wrong speech is called right speech.
The abandonment of the three kinds of wrong action is called right action.
The abandonment of unwholesome wrong livelihood is called right livelihood.
To contemplate with diligent effort therein is called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
To contemplate therein with mindfulness and non-forgetfulness is called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
To abide with a single-pointed mind therein is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
This is called the Eightfold Noble Path leading to Nirvana.
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, tranquility, equanimity, reflection, and virtue—these ten factors are explained as thirty-seven when analyzed.
Faith in the Dharma is called the faculty of faith and the power of faith;
diligence is the faculty of diligence, the power of diligence, the four right efforts, the factor of enlightenment of diligence, and right exertion;
the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, right mindfulness, and the joy of the factor of enlightenment of joy.

Wisdom (*prajñā*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the factor of awakening of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); serenity (*praśrabdhi*), the factor of awakening of serenity (*praśrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga*);

concentration (*samādhi*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the factor of awakening of concentration (*samādhisaṃbodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
Vigilance is the awakening factor of vigilance;
reflection is right intention;
and ethical discipline consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right exertion.
The abiding in the four kinds of wisdom is called *smṛtyupasthāna* (establishment of mindfulness).
Upright diligence is called *samyakprahāṇa* (right exertion).
Abiding with a single mind without distraction within the objects of focus is called the four *ṛddhipāda* (bases of psychic power).
Those arising within the minds of persons of dull faculties are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Those arising within the minds of persons of sharp faculties are called the five powers (*pañcabala*).
Within the path of seeing the truths (*darśanamārga*), they are called the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
Within the path of contemplation, these are called the seven factors of enlightenment.
These ten dharmas subsume the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
In the stage of *anāgamya-dhyāna*, there are thirty-six, excluding the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The stage of the second dhyāna also consists of thirty-six factors, excluding *vitarka* (direct thought).
In the third, fourth, and intermediate dhyānas, there are thirty-five factors, excluding *prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga* (joy as a factor of enlightenment) and *vitarka*.
In the first dhyāna, there are thirty-seven factors.

In the three formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi), there are thirty-two, excluding the awakening factor of joy (prīti-sambodhyaṅga) and the right [aspects of] thought (samyak-saṃkalpa), speech (vāc), action (karmānta), and livelihood (ājīva).
In the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), there are twenty-two, excluding the seven awakening factors and the eight factors of the Path (mārgāṅga).
The desire realm also consists of twenty-two [factors], excluding the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path.
Chapter 15: The Four Truths. *Abhidharma-amṛta-rasa*, Chapter Ten-Four: The Four Truths. The four truths are:
the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
It is of one kind:
the characteristic of affliction constitutes suffering.
Two kinds: physical suffering and mental suffering.
Three kinds:
The suffering of suffering, the suffering of separation, and the suffering of conditioned impermanence.
There are four kinds:
internal and external physical suffering, and internal and external mental suffering.
Fivefold: the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Sixfold:
The suffering of the three realms and the suffering of the three poisons.
Seven kinds: the suffering of the seven stations of consciousness.
The eight kinds of suffering:
birth, aging, sickness, death, association with the disliked, separation from the beloved, not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of all manner of various things.
This is called the Truth of Suffering.
What is the Truth of Origination?
These five aggregates of clinging, which are the causes of these various forms of suffering, are called the Truth of Origination.
What is the truth of cessation?
The complete and remainderless extinction of suffering and its origin, which is the object of knowledge and the cessation [of defilements], is called the truth of cessation.
Practicing the eightfold noble path is called the truth of the path.
Regarding these Four Noble Truths, one should know them in their proper sequence as that which is to be abandoned and realized.
When one contemplates their true nature for oneself and truly attains the fruit and becomes a practitioner who is not deceptive, this is called "Truth" (satya).
The sequence is established according to the coarseness of the cognitions.
The Truth of Suffering is coarse and easy to recognize; therefore, it is the first Truth of Suffering.
Having recognized suffering, one investigates its cause, which arises from the Truth of Origination; therefore, the Truth of Origination is second.
Where is this Truth of Suffering extinguished so that liberation is attained?
By contemplating within Nirvāṇa; for this reason, the Truth of Cessation is third.
How is this cessation to be attained?
By contemplating and practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one severs the fetters and brings the Truth of Cessation to fulfillment; for this reason, the Truth of the Path is the fourth.
When the five aggregates of clinging manifest as the fruit of retribution, this is called the Truth of Suffering.

When the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) arise through causes and conditions, this is called the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) and is also called the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya), just as a person may be called both "son" and "father.
The Truth of Origination consists mostly of the fetters and afflictions (saṃyojana-kleśa).
What are the fetters? There are nine fetters:
the fetter of craving, ill-will, conceit, ignorance, doubt, views, wrong resolve, stinginess, and envy.
The desire for the three realms is the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
The agitation of anger and malice within the minds of sentient beings is the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
The seven types of pride are the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*).
The delusion bound to the three realms is the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
The three views are the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Two views are the fetter of wrong resolve (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Lack of certainty regarding the Four Noble Truths is the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
A mind that is stingy, covetous, and miserly is the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
To harbor resentment toward others out of envy is the fetter of jealousy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is of two kinds:

first, the exhaustion of fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); second, the exhaustion of fetters and latent tendencies through the path without outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*).
There are various pure phenomena (*viśuddhi-dharma*), such as the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Dharma, expression, eloquence, and meaning.
To know the true nature of all names and designations is called the analytical knowledge of Dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
To possess the wisdom regarding all speech and discourse is called the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*).
To know the true nature of all phenomena is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
All wisdom, speech, meditative concentration, supernormal powers, and knowledge is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).
The four unshakable faiths of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) are: [faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts].
Unshakable faith in the Buddha, unshakable faith in the Dharma, unshakable faith in the Saṅgha, and unshakable faith in the pure precepts.
The fruit of arhatship encompasses all the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The untainted faith within the various great merits of the Buddha is called "unshakable faith in the Buddha.

The untainted faith within nirvāṇa, within the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training among the untainted truths, and within the true merits of the bodhisattvas—this purity of untainted faith is called "unshakable faith in the Dharma."

Having attained the fruits of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one has faith in all the merits of the four pairs and eight ranks (*catur-yugāṣṭa-pudgala*); this faith, which is placed in the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples and not elsewhere, is called "unbreakable faith in the Saṃgha."
The non-informative (avijñapti) untainted precepts are herein the untainted faith; this is called "unshakable faith in the precepts.
When pure and true wisdom is conjoined with faith, for this reason no one can surpass these untainted precepts; therefore, it is unshakable faith.
These are called the four unshakable faiths.
There are four matters for the cultivation of concentration:

cultivating concentration to attain a pleasant dwelling in the present life; cultivating concentration to attain knowledge and vision; cultivating concentration to attain analytical wisdom; and cultivating concentration to attain the various virtues of the exhaustion of the outflows.
The first dhyāna can attain a dwelling in happiness in the present;
the supernormal knowledge of the wisdom of birth and death is called "knowledge and vision.
Seeking merit through skillful means refers to the unmanifest precepts of the desire realm and the merits of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
All phenomena of the realm of form and the formless realm, as well as all conditioned phenomena that are untainted (*anāsrava*), are called "discriminative wisdom" (*prajñā-vibhakti*).

The diamond-like fourth dhyāna, which is associated with the final mind of training (*śaikṣa-citta*) and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), is called "attaining the exhaustion of outflows through the cultivation of concentration" (*samādhi-bhāvanā-āsravakṣaya*).
Included within the fourth dhyāna are the four paths: the difficult-to-know suffering, the easy-to-know suffering, the difficult-to-know pleasure, and the easy-to-know pleasure.

The untainted dharmas of the faith-follower with dull faculties are the difficult-to-know suffering; the untainted dharmas of the dharma-follower with sharp faculties are the easy-to-know suffering; and the dharmas of both sharp and dull faculties within the fundamental fourth dhyāna are called the path of pleasure.
Why is this? Because the paths of śamatha and vipaśyanā are equal.
Since the degrees of śamatha and vipaśyanā differ across other stages, these are described as suffering.

In the two stages of the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the path of stillness (*śamatha*) is slight while the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*) is predominant.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the path of insight is slight while the path of stillness is predominant; this is called "suffering," because the path is difficult to attain.
The seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*):

first, the various devas and humans within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the Brahmakāyika devas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—excluding those devas who have just been reborn therein—possess different bodies and different perceptions (*nānātva-kāya-nānātva-saṃjñin*).
2. The gods of the Brahmakāyika realm, newly born, have diverse bodies but a single perception.
3. The gods born in the second dhyāna have a single body but diverse perceptions.
4. The gods born in the third dhyāna have a single body and a single perception.

Fifth, the gods born in the sphere of infinite space; sixth, the gods born in the sphere of infinite consciousness; seventh, the gods born in the sphere of nothingness—these are called the seven stations of consciousness. Why is this so?

Because consciousness is not destroyed [therein]. In the miserable realms (*apāya*), consciousness is destroyed by the suffering and pain; therefore, they are not established as abodes of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
In the fourth dhyāna, because the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) destroys consciousness, it is likewise not established as an abode of consciousness.
Because consciousness is destroyed in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and in the attainment of cessation, these cannot be established as stations of consciousness.
As for the nine abodes of sentient beings:

these seven stations of consciousness, along with the non-percipient beings and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are called the nine abodes of sentient beings because sentient beings dwell within them.

Robes, food and drink, and bedding; delighting in the severance of the fetters (saṃyojana); and attaining the Path through the power of contemplation on conditions—these are called the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Contentment with robes, food and drink, and bedding, whether they be of good or poor quality—these are the [first] three noble lineages.
The suffering of seeking what one lacks, the suffering of guarding what one has, and the suffering of losing it—these are the three sufferings that cause one to lose the path of goodness.
Life cannot be sustained without food; for this reason, one should come to know contentment.
When these three sufferings are lost and desire is abandoned, one attains joy and gladness within the mind; this is called the fourth [joy].
The hundred and eight kinds of painful sensations arise from the contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six contacts (*ṣaḍ-sparśāḥ*).
There are three types:
when the eye sees forms, there is sorrow, joy, or equanimity; and so on, up to when the mind attends to mental objects (*dharma*), there is sorrow, joy, or equanimity.
Within these, there are wholesome and unwholesome states.
There are eighteen wholesome and eighteen unwholesome, which are called the thirty-six.
These three types constitute the one hundred and eight.
There are thirty-six [factors] of the past, thirty-six of the future, and thirty-six of the present.
Because the five consciousnesses cannot perform discrimination, there is neither sorrow nor joy therein.
When mental formations and mental factors continue in succession without interruption and are constantly recollected within the mind, this is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
By following the conditions of these phenomena through recollection, and because the power of recollective awareness becomes strong through repeated conditioning, one does not forget past phenomena.
The eye, the person, the mind, and mental factors exist as seen in a dream through causes and conditions; there is no seeing in a dream without causes or conditions.
Whether this dream belongs to the past or to the future, it is likewise so.
If one sees in a dream a person growing horns, these are originally the horns of an ox; one then forcefully reflects:
"Why does a human not grow horns?
Having thought thus, one sees in the dream a person growing horns.
A distracted and disordered mind is called delusion (*moha*).
This delusion may arise due to physical illness, due to possession by malevolent spirits, or due to causal conditions from previous lives.
There are three factors:
The factors of morality (*śīlāṅga*), the factors of concentration (*samādhyaṅga*), and the factors of wisdom (*prajñāṅga*). What are the factors of morality?
They are the manifest and unmanifest precepts of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the unmanifest precepts of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
What are the factors of concentration?
They are the cultivation of the fourteen concentrations.
What are the factors of wisdom?
The three kinds of wisdom are:
that derived from hearing, that derived from reflection, and that derived from cultivation.
In the desire realm, there are two kinds:
Hearing and reflection.
In the form realm, there are two types:
hearing and reflection.
In the formless realm, there is one kind:
mental cultivation.
There are two kinds of restraint:
First, the restraint of the mind;
second, the restraint of the precepts.
What is the restraint of the mind?
One must not give rise to lust, maintaining the perception of women as one's mother or the like, or as sisters or daughters;
upon seeing a woman, one should not dwell on her, nor give rise to thoughts regarding her female organs, for from this arise many sins and afflictions.
Contemplating that the mind and body are detached from these [defilements] is called the restraint of conduct (*śīla-saṃvara*).

To eliminate various unwholesome states such as sexual desire, to not violate the precepts and remain free from blemish, and to purify the mind of defilement by cleansing the seven types of lustful desire—this is called the restraint of morality (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Afflictions, evil karma, and the retribution of evil karma constitute these three obstructions.
These are the extremely heavy afflictions of the karmic offenses against the [Three Jewels] and the retribution of the three evil realms.
If even one of these three things is present, one does not receive the Noble Dharma; therefore, they are called obstructions.
There are three kinds of unwholesome applied and sustained thought:
sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness.
These destroy the three kinds of wholesome applied and sustained thought.
No lust, no anger, and no delusion.
The three kinds of afflictions are:
lust, anger, and delusion.
This illness has three kinds of medicine:
the contemplation of the impurity of the body, loving-kindness toward sentient beings, and the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination; these are called the three medicines.

By cultivating the body, cultivating morality, cultivating the mind, and cultivating wisdom, one will not receive any evil retribution through these dharmas, or will receive only a slight retribution, whether in this life or in future lives.
How does one cultivate the body?
By contemplating various aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
How does one cultivate ethical discipline?
Maintain the precepts without transgression and constantly guard them.
How does one cultivate the mind?
By eliminating unwholesome thoughts and reflections, and practicing wholesome thoughts and reflections.
What is the cultivation of wisdom?
It is the increase of wisdom through various kinds of discernment of wholesome dharmas.
One who practices what is wholesome easily attains the good path; one who practices what is unwholesome easily falls into the evil path.
There may be virtuous people who fall into evil realms, or there may be wicked people who are born into good realms.

This is because the residual retribution from powerful causes and conditions in previous lives has not yet been exhausted; thus, depending on whether one's final mind at the time of death is wholesome or unwholesome, a virtuous person may fall into an evil realm, while an unwholesome person may be born into a good realm.
16. Chapter on Miscellaneous Topics: The Essence of the Ambrosia of Abhidharma. Chapter Sixteen on Miscellaneous Topics. The four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
the six dharmas, the five aggregates, and the extinction through wisdom—these are called the analysis of the four fruits.
The fruit of arhatship is comprised within nine stages, excluding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The third fruit is comprised within six stages, excluding the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is absent therein.
The Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin are included within the stage of the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna), because they have not yet abandoned desire for the human body.
There are four inversions:
the inversion of mind, the inversion of perception, and the inversion of view, which consist of perceiving permanence in what is impermanent.
To perceive pleasure in suffering, purity in the impure, and a self in what is not-self constitutes a perversion of mind, a perversion of perception, and a perversion of view.
All such perversions are abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Why is this? The three views that subsume the perversions regarding the basis of suffering conditioned by formations are:
the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the misapprehension of views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
All sixty-two views are subsumed within five false views:
to perceive a real self within the five aggregates where no real self exists is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
to rely on the notions of permanence or annihilation while failing to understand causes, conditions, and karmic retribution is the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
To hold that the true Dharma lacks this world and the next world, lacks *nirvāṇa* and the Four Noble Truths, and so forth, is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

To perceive what is not truly pleasant or pure as being pleasant and pure—like seeing a felled tree standing upright at night from a distance and mistaking it for a person—is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To perceive what is not a cause as a cause, and to perceive what is not the path as the path, is the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering, because one conceives of a self within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

The notion of permanence and the notion of annihilation are abandoned through the Truth of Suffering, because they take the present five aggregates as their object; this is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

If one regards suffering as true and abandons it through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and likewise regards origin, cessation, and the path as true and abandons them through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path (*samudaya-nirodha-mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), this refers to the abandonment of the view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

If, within the truth of suffering, one calculates [it] as having pleasure or purity, this is abandoned through the vision of suffering; likewise, if within origin, cessation, and the path one calculates [them] as having pleasure or purity, this is abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path.

The "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of seeking *nirvāṇa* through non-ways and viewing what is not a cause as a cause; this is the clinging to precepts, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).

There are six types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by abandonment (*prahāṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by removal (*vibhāvana-bhāvanā*), cultivation by discernment (*paricaya-bhāvanā*), and cultivation by restraint (*saṃvara-bhāvanā*).
How is cultivation attained?
One attains previously unattained wholesome dharmas and merits; having attained them, all other remaining merits are also attained.
How is it practiced?
Having previously attained various merits, one now practices them in the present.
What is meant by "abandoning through cultivation"? It is the abandonment of all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) through wholesome dharmas.
What is cultivation by removal?
It is that which can eliminate all unwholesome dharmas.
What is analytical cultivation?
One discerningly contemplates the true mark of the body.
How is restraint cultivated?
Because the objects of the six sense-faculties are powerful and defiling.

Regarding the five faculties: the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is extinguished without remainder in the first dhyāna; the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is extinguished without remainder in the second dhyāna; the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is extinguished without remainder in the third dhyāna; the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is extinguished without remainder in the fourth dhyāna; and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is extinguished without remainder in the samādhi of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*).
The three realms:
the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the realm of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
The abandonment of all other afflictions (*kleśa*) with the exception of the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇāsaṃyojana*) is called the realm of abandonment.
The severance of the fetter of craving is called the realm of desirelessness (*vītarāga-dhātu*).
The severance of all other phenomena is called the realm of exhaustion (*kṣaya-dhātu*).
By extinguishing sensual desire, one attains liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*); by extinguishing ignorance, one attains liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
The internal and external sense bases are not bound to one another; it is sensual desire that acts as the bond.
It is like two oxen tied together by a yoke. For this reason, one should guard the mind amidst objects of attraction and aversion, and should not harbor a mind of attachment or hatred.
Ten dharmas:
the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, the untainted, the associated, the dissociated, wholesome unconditioned, and indeterminate unconditioned.
These are called the ten dharmas.
Five dharmas have dharma-knowledge as their object.
What are the five?
The factors associated with and dissociated from the desire realm, the factors associated with and dissociated from the untainted, and the wholesome unconditioned factors—
these are the five factors.
The knowledge of the unknown takes these seven factors as its object.
What are the seven? They are:

phenomena associated with and dissociated from the form realm; phenomena associated with and dissociated from the formless realm; untainted phenomena associated with and dissociated from [the mind]; and wholesome unconditioned phenomena.
The knowledge of others' minds takes three types of phenomena as its object:
associated phenomena bound to the desire realm, associated phenomena bound to the form realm, and associated untainted phenomena.
Conventional knowledge takes ten types of phenomena as its object:

Factors associated with and dissociated from the desire realm; factors associated with and dissociated from the form realm; factors associated with and dissociated from the formless realm; untainted factors associated with and dissociated [from the mind]; wholesome unconditioned phenomena; and indeterminate unconditioned phenomena.
The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) each take six factors as their objects:
the associated and dissociated factors bound to the three realms; these are called the six factors.
The knowledge of cessation (*kṣaya-jñāna*) takes one factor as its object: the wholesome unconditioned factor (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
The knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) takes two types of phenomena as its objects:
untainted associated phenomena and dissociated phenomena.
The knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) take nine types of phenomena as their objects, excluding indeterminate unconditioned phenomena.

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of a given level are permeated by the proclivities (*anuśaya*) of that same level; the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are pervasive throughout both their own level and other levels; all others are permeated by the proclivities of their own respective levels.
There are two kinds of phenomena:
associated phenomena and dissociated phenomena.
What are associated phenomena?
Regarding all minds and mental factors:
what are the dissociated phenomena? They are the seventeen dharmas, beginning with acquisition (prāpti).
The seventeen dharmas are:
first, accomplishment;
second, the attainment of non-conception;
3. The attainment of cessation;
4. the state of non-perception;
5. the life-faculty;
Sixth, by way of category;
seventh, by way of acquisition through location;
eighth, by way of acquisition through substance.
9. Entering [the womb]; 10. Birth; 11. Aging;
12. Abiding; 13. Impermanence; 14. The Aggregate of Names;
15. The aggregate of letters;
16. The aggregate of tastes;
17. The nature of ordinary beings.
When one attains the various dharmas, those factors dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) are attained simultaneously; this is called "attainment" (prāpti).

Disgusted with the notions of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, through the power of the four dhyānas, for a certain duration one causes the cessation of mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma); this is called the "attainment of non-ideation" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).

Weary of toil and humiliation, one brings to rest the perception of cessation; through the meditative power of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, for a certain duration, the mind and mental factors are extinguished—this is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

When the mind and mental factors do not function and are suspended within those born in the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*), this is called the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñikāyatana*).
The continuity of the four great elements and the various faculties without disruption is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The similarity in body, mind, and speech among other sentient beings within various places of birth is called the category of sentient beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
That which is obtained upon reaching another land or region is called "acquisition by place" (sthāna-pratilambha).
The various conditioned phenomena and miscellaneous objects are called "acquisition by thing" (vastu-pratilambha).
The acquisition of all internal and external sense bases (āyatana) is called "acquisition by base" (āyatana-pratilambha).

The arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is birth; the maturation of these phenomena is aging; the non-extinction of these phenomena is abiding; and the extinction of these phenomena is impermanence. The collection of names (*nāmakāya*) consists of the combination of syllables;

the collection of phrases (*padakāya*) consists of the combination of names used to express a matter; and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) consists of the combination of extensive explanations.
Not yet having attained the noble, untainted path, this is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This is called the seventeenth.
Among these mental non-associated factors (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
Two are wholesome, seven are indeterminate, and eight are to be analyzed.
The attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation are called wholesome.

The state of non-perception, the generic characteristics (*jāti*), the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), the collection of syllables (*vyañjanakāya*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) are called indeterminate.
Accomplishment, birth, aging, abiding, and impermanence—whether among the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate—are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate respectively.
Likewise, acquisition of the bases (*āyatana-lābha*), acquisition of things (*vastu-lābha*), and acquisition of the spheres (*dhātu-lābha*) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

How many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Three are bound to the desire realm, two are bound to the form realm, one is bound to the formless realm; eleven are to be analyzed as being either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
The collection of names, the collection of phrases, and the collection of syllables are bound to the realms of desire and form.
The attainment of non-perception and the state of non-perception are bound to the realm of form.
The attainment of cessation is bound to the formless realm.

Accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), genus (*nikāyasabhāga*), acquisition of bases (*āyatanaprāpti*), acquisition of entities (*vastuprāpti*), acquisition of entrances (*dhātuprāpti*), and the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) are bound to the three realms.

Birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*) are bound to the desire realm among phenomena bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm among phenomena bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm among phenomena bound to the formless realm, and unbound among phenomena that are unbound.
Among these, how many are with-outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without-outflows (anāsrava)?
Thirteen are with-outflows; four are to be analyzed.
Birth, aging, duration, and impermanence are with-outflows when they pertain to that which has outflows, and without-outflows when they pertain to that which is without outflows.
Upon attaining the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), one abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
When being born into another realm, one likewise abandons the nature of an ordinary person and acquires the nature of an ordinary person belonging to that other realm.
It is severed during the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) at the time of becoming free from desire.
What are the three unconditioned phenomena?
They are the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*).
What is the cessation through wisdom?
When the power of wisdom—both with-outflows and without-outflows—severs all fetters and latent tendencies, one attains liberation; this is called "extinction conditioned by wisdom.
What is "extinction not conditioned by wisdom"?
That which is the non-arising of future conditioned phenomena is called cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). What is space?
That which is formless, non-obstructive, and invisible is called space.

The co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the concomitant cause (*sahagata-hetu*) arise first; being their own similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) while not yet having arisen, they subsequently serve as causes for all other dharmas.
Thus, the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is also a sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).
Among sentient beings, there are retributive causes; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are both the fruits of conditioned phenomena and the fruit of nirvāṇa. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and the factors associated with the path to nirvāṇa proceed simultaneously within a single condition.
Within other-characteristics and not within self-characteristics, the mind and mental factors have no location and no spatial direction. Why is this?
Because they take all places as their objects.
When the Path arises, the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and proclivities (*anuśaya*) are about to be extinguished; therefore, by the arising of the Path, one attains liberation.

When the Path does not yet cease, the desire [to be liberated] is about to be extinguished; the Path of Non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the fetters and proclivities, and through the arising of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one attains liberation.
There are three kinds of craving:
craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
The seeking and pursuit of various objects is called craving for sensual pleasure.
To covet and cherish when something is obtained is called craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
To seek its cessation through vision and to sever it through abandonment is called non-craving for existence (*vibhavarāga*).

Among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), with the exception of right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), the remainder are the factors of the faculties (*indriya-dharma*).
Each of the four foundations of mindfulness manifests before one.
Why is this? Because they analytically discern all phenomena as objects of perception.
All phenomena are associated with others but not with themselves; among these phenomena, the fetters that are to be abandoned through conditions must be relinquished—this is called "abandonment.
There is abandonment that is not yet disjunction. What is abandonment that is not yet disjunction?

One who has attained the knowledge of suffering but not yet attained the knowledge of origination [abandons] that which is to be abandoned by the truth of origination and that which is to be abandoned by the truth of suffering.

Regarding the three truths, one attains two unshakable faiths: unshakable faith in the Dharma and unshakable faith in the precepts, with respect to the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, and the truth of cessation.
Within the Truth of the Path, one attains the four unshakable faiths; all mental factors (caitta-dharma) follow the mind because they share a single object (ālambana).
Likewise, the unmanifest precepts (avijñapti-śīla) that arise, abide, age, and perish follow the mind. All contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) are to be abandoned.
Why is this? Because of the defilement of transgressions.
One should know that all phenomena, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), are likewise affected.
Why is this? Wisdom takes all phenomena as its object.
The phenomena of the past and future are distant.
Why is this? Because they do not accomplish the task.
Present phenomena are proximate.
Why is this? Because it accomplishes the task; thus, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is also proximate.
Why is this? Because they are swiftly attained.
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are objects of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), because they serve as the objective conditions (*ālambana*) for the five views.

At a minimum, nineteen faculties are attained: one whose mental faculty is unimpaired and who possesses two sexual organs; likewise, a person who has seen the truths (dṛṣṭasatya), whose mental faculty is unimpaired but who has not yet abandoned desire—these are said to possess nineteen.
At least eight faculties are severed when one cuts off the roots of goodness.
When dying gradually, there remains the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Furthermore, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is contact (*sparśa*) through the conjunction of the three factors: the sense organ, the object, and consciousness.
This contact is of five kinds:

contact through resistance (*pratigha*), contact through designation (*adhivacana*), contact through clarity (*vidyā*), contact through ignorance (*avidyā*), and contact that is neither clarity nor ignorance.
That which is associated with the five consciousnesses is called contact through resistance.
That which is associated with mental consciousness is called "designation.
Defiled contact is called "ignorance.
Untainted contact is called "knowledge."
Untainted and with-outflow contact is called "neither knowledge nor ignorance.
Through two paths one attains the fruit: first, the severing of the fetters and latent tendencies; [second, the cultivation of the path].
2. Attainment of Liberation.
An Arhat enters parinirvāṇa through the retributive mind, because all phenomena have been relinquished. There are four modes of existence (bhava):
There are birth-existence (upapatti-bhava), death-existence (maraṇa-bhava), fundamental existence (pūrva-kāla-bhava), and intermediate existence (antarā-bhava).
The acquisition of the five aggregates at the moment of initial birth is called birth-existence.
The five aggregates at the time of death are called death-existence.
Excluding birth and death, that which exists within the five aggregates is called "original existence" (*pūrvabhava*).
That which, after death, is able to reach the five aggregates of the various realms of rebirth is called "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*).

The knowledge and patience regarding the truths of suffering and its origin, taking all phenomena as their object, is called "disgust" (*nirveda*), because it takes objects of disgust as its condition.
Among the four truths, the various knowledges (*jñāna*) and patiences (*kṣānti*) constitute the departure from desire, because desire is extinguished.
There are three outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of desire (*kāma*), the outflow of existence (*bhava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā*).
In the desire realm, with the exception of ignorance, the remaining afflictions are called the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
In the form and formless realms, with the exception of ignorance, the remaining afflictions are the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*).
The delusion bound to the three realms is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
When all these outflows are completely exhausted, at that time one attains the exhaustion of all suffering.
One attains the nectar-like flavor of omniscience; this was composed by the noble one named Ghoṣa who attained the Path.
